Think of memory as a toy box. The garbage collector can recycle unreachable toys. A file handle is more like a borrowed key: return it promptly, rather than waiting for a cleanup day.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

What the runtime does

  • Managed objects live on the managed heap. Roots include active local references, statics and references reachable from them. Unreachable objects can be collected; a value going out of scope does not promise an immediate collection.
  • Generations 0, 1 and 2 group objects by survival. Collection may move objects and update references. Large objects are handled specially. Do not depend on collection timing for program correctness.
  • IDisposable.Dispose releases owned resources such as streams and connections. using is a try/finally shortcut. await using works with IAsyncDisposable. The GC does not call Dispose for you.
  • A finalizer is a fallback for unmanaged-resource ownership, not a normal cleanup timer. Prefer SafeHandle over writing a raw finalizer. Avoid GC.Collect in everyday application code.

Read the example

using (var writer = new StreamWriter("lifetime.txt"))
{
    writer.WriteLine("Saved safely");
}
Console.WriteLine(File.ReadAllText("lifetime.txt").Trim());

Expected line: Saved safely. StreamWriter opens the file; WriteLine writes text; leaving the block closes the writer even if the block throws. System.IO is built into .NET, so no extra NuGet package is needed.

Try it yourself

Why can an unclosed file stay locked even when you no longer use the variable?

Worked answer

The reference becoming unreachable does not guarantee immediate finalization. Close your owned stream with using.

Change the code to append two lines.

Worked answer

Use File.AppendAllText("lifetime.txt", "First\nSecond\n"). ReadAllLines returns one string per line.
